title: Gmail Monday Integration: How to Set It Up (2026)
summary: Gmail monday integration connects email to tasks via no-code workflows. You'll determine which email events should automatically create or update tasks.
body_markdown:
## Build a Gmail-monday.com workflow step by step


Build it in four stages, each ending with something that works: a trigger chosen, both accounts connected, two fields mapped, and a real item on the board. The list below shows the order, and the stages after it give the detail for each.


1. Connect Gmail.
2. Connect monday.com.
3. Pick the board and group.
4. Map subject and sender.
5. Test.
6. Publish.
7. Check the item arrived.


Keep to that order. If a step fails, you know which stage broke it. Next come the stages themselves.


You can also skip the clicking: describe the workflow to the built-in chat in Activepieces, say a labelled Gmail message should create an item on one monday.com board, and it publishes the same flow you would have assembled by hand.


What it publishes is a live flow in your account, wired from Gmail and monday.com integrations that are two of the 750 integrations counted directly from the open source monorepo.


The run trace for each execution records the subject and sender of the email that triggered it and the monday.com item that came out, so the result is something you read rather than take on trust.


It runs under the same RBAC and audit logs as any flow built manually. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run an open source automation platform of this kind in production.


Create a new workflow and pick Gmail's "New Email" as the only trigger. Don't add a filter yet. An unfiltered trigger shows you immediately whether Gmail is delivering anything at all, which a filter would hide if it were wrong.


### Stage 2: Connect your monday.com and Gmail accounts


Connect Gmail first, then monday.com. Each opens an authorization dialog. Take a screenshot of that dialog before you click Allow, because it lists the permissions you are granting.


If a connection fails, the error text in that dialog is the evidence to keep, and it tells you more than "it did not work" does.


Use a mailbox you can send test messages to. A shared inbox you don't control makes the later check unreliable.


### Add the monday.com action and map Gmail fields


Add monday.com's "Create Item" as the single action. Choose the board, then the group the item should land in. Then map two fields: item name takes the email's subject, and a text column on your board takes the sender's address.


If the sender column is a different column type, such as a people column, the mapping may be rejected or leave the cell empty. Use a plain text column for this first run.


Take a screenshot of the field-mapping panel with both values filled, so you can compare it against the result.


### Test and publish your Gmail-monday.com workflow


Send yourself an email with a distinctive subject, run the test, and capture the test result screen. It should show the subject and sender the trigger picked up. Publish only after that looks right.


Then verify outside the builder. Send one more email, open the monday.com board, and look in the group you chose. The item should carry that subject as its name and the sender in the text column.


If the item is missing, check the trigger's run history first. That tells you whether the email was never seen or the item was never created.
